title: No idols
hookLine: don't make God small enough to carry

lines: A BURDEN TO THE WEARY BEAST.
IT STAYS WHERE YOU PUT IT.
cards: A procession is moving, and the gods are riding on pack animals. In Isaiah, the images of Bel and Nebo are loaded onto beasts and cattle: "your carriages were heavy loaden; they are a burden to the weary beast."

Then he describes what people do with a god they've made. "They bear him upon the shoulder, they carry him, and set him in his place, and he standeth; from his place shall he not remove." A god you have to haul around.
A god that stays exactly where you put it.

teach.h: A GOD CUT DOWN TO SIZE.
teach.b: The commandment says it plainly: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image." Orthodox and Reformed Christians count it as a word of its own; Catholics and Lutherans read it as part of the first.
Either way, the worry is the same. An idol is a god cut down to size. You made it, so it can't surprise you.

You set it down, so it stays put. And Isaiah turns the picture over. A few verses earlier, God speaks: "even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you."
Churches have drawn the line on images in different places. Orthodox Christians fill their churches with icons and venerate them, with a firm line between honoring an image and worshipping it.
Catholics use statues and paintings and teach, as the Orthodox do, that the honor passes to the one shown. Reformed churches have tended to keep worship plain, wary of images in worship at all.
Each is taking the same warning seriously. But the commandment reaches past wood and paint.
A god can be carved out of ideas, too: a God who shares all your opinions, likes exactly the people you like, never asks for anything inconvenient.

teach.h: A GOD THAT FITS IN A POCKET.
teach.b: That god fits in a pocket. The God of Isaiah doesn't. "To whom will ye liken me?" he asks, and a few verses later the answer comes: "I am God, and there is none like me."

how: Christians apply this commandment differently: Orthodox churches are filled with icons that believers venerate, Catholic churches use statues and paintings, and Reformed churches tend to keep worship spaces plain; preachers in each often extend it to the ideas people make of God.

o: a rule against keeping photos of loved ones
a ban on admiring well-known people too much
not shrinking God into something made or carried

games.q: carried or carrying — tap the pairs.
p: I will carry, and will deliver you

s: Catholics and Lutherans leave out the verse about images
they read it as part of the first word. the words are the same.
in Isaiah 46, the idols are carried and God carries
"even I will carry, and will deliver you."
Isaiah's idol moves about wherever it's needed
"from his place shall he not remove."

games.q: you're Isaiah, watching the images of Bel and Nebo sway past on tired animals. what do you point out?
o: how beautifully the images are made.
that these gods have to be carried, while God carries his people.
that the procession is far too long.
games.why: the idols are "a burden to the weary beast." God says instead: "I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry."

practice: Ask quietly: where does God always seem to agree with me, and which people do I picture God not bothering with?

Let one pocket-sized picture come up and notice its edges, then set Isaiah's question beside it: to whom will ye liken me? If you pray, you can sit with that question before God, without rushing to answer.

wordCard.voice: No idols. Not making God small enough to carry, in wood or stone, or in the ideas we keep in our pockets.

orig.note: Hebrew: a carved image. The graven image of Exodus 20:4.

carryVoice: Your line: god is bigger. Bigger than any picture we can carry. Go gently.
